title: Until 1989, Hungarian school books called the revolution of 1956 a ‘counter-revolution’
body: After the Soviet army crushed the revolution, János Kádár ruled Hungary until 1988. First came reprisals: thousands were jailed, and Imre Nagy was hanged on 16 June 1958. Then Kádár offered a bargain: ‘whoever is not against us is with us’ (1961). In December 1962 the UN dropped ‘the Hungarian question’ after a secret understanding with Washington, and in March 1963 Kádár announced an amnesty that freed most of those jailed for 1956, though several hundred stayed in prison ([Békés and Kecskés, eds.](https://www.mek.oszk.hu/12900/12960/12960.pdf)). The New Economic Mechanism of 1968 brought some market rules into the planned economy, and living standards rose: by the Statistical Office’s figures real wages were half as high again in 1975 as in 1960, before falling in the 1980s ([KSH](https://www.ksh.hu/evkonyvek/2023/magyar-statisztikai-evkonyv-2023/pdf/statevk2023_1.pdf)). The other side of the bargain was **silence**: in school books 1956 was a ‘counter-revolution’, by the 1980s ‘the regrettable events’. On 28 January 1989 the minister Imre Pozsgay called it a ‘popular uprising’, and on 16 June 1989 Imre Nagy was reburied before some 200,000 people.

slides.question: By Hungary’s Statistical Office, what were real wages in 1975 as a percentage of their 1960 level?
slides.explanation: 152%: half as high again. Real income per head almost doubled (199). Real wages peaked in 1980 at 158 and fell to 142 by 1990.

slides.alt: Animation in faded paper and olive: a bar of the Kádár era from 1956 to 1988, the reprisals, the slogan on a sheet of paper, a pair of scales with the UN deal and the amnesty, a steaming pot of goulash, the official real-wage and real-income curves, and a school book whose word for 1956 changes.
slides.music: “Long Note Four” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Move through the official figures, 1960 to 1990, and find when real wages stopped rising.
slides.takeaway: In 1980, at 158. By 1990 real wages had fallen to 142, while real income per head kept rising: the material side of the bargain weakened in the 1980s.

slides.question: In 1962–63, what did Hungary’s rulers get in return for an amnesty for those jailed after 1956?
options: A seat on the UN Security Council
slides.explanation: A secret Hungarian–US understanding: the UN General Assembly took the question off its agenda on 20 December 1962, and Kádár announced the amnesty on 21 March 1963.
